planting.note: Plant rooted cuttings or container trees in spring once soil has warmed; Bhagwa flowers and sets fruit across three separate bloom cycles in its native climate, so expect an extended, staggered harvest window rather than one single crop.

directions: Bhagwa is the dominant commercial pomegranate cultivar of Maharashtra, India, prized for a vivid saffron-red rind, deep red glossy arils, and soft, easily chewed seeds that make it a favorite for both fresh eating and export markets. It was formally released as 'Phule Bhagwa' by an Indian agricultural university breeding program and performs best with a hot, dry ripening period, so in the humid Gulf South it benefits from wider plant spacing, good airflow, and prompt removal of any cracked or fungal-affected fruit. Trees are self-fertile and productive but tend toward heavier disease pressure than drier-climate selections when grown in high-humidity gardens. Give full sun and sharp drainage, and expect the first meaningful crop three to five years after planting.
sources: Mahatma Phule Krishi Vidyapeeth (MPKV), Rahuri — Phule Bhagwa Pomegranate Release
ICAR-National Research Centre on Pomegranate
Texas A&M AgriLife Extension — Pomegranates for Texas

planting.note: Plant rooted cuttings or container trees in spring in full sun; Ganesh sets fruit reliably on its own so no second cultivar is needed for pollination.

directions: Selected near Pune, India in the mid-20th century, Ganesh was for decades the leading pomegranate cultivar in Indian home orchards and retail markets before being partly displaced by later selections such as Bhagwa and Mridula. Fruit is medium-sized with a pink-blushed skin and soft, sweet-tart pink arils, and the tree bears dependably once established, making it a good dooryard choice for growers who want a well-proven heirloom rather than a newer commercial release. Like other Indian selections, quality and fruit-skin condition are best where the ripening period stays hot and relatively dry, so thin overcrowded branches to maximize airflow in humid Gulf Coast plantings. It remains widely available through fruit-tree specialty nurseries as an older, still-respected cultivar.
sources: Mahatma Phule Krishi Vidyapeeth (MPKV), Rahuri — Pomegranate Cultivar Records

planting.note: Plant rooted cuttings or container trees in spring in full sun and well-drained soil; Mridula is more vigorous than its parent cultivar Ganesh and benefits from early structural pruning to keep fruiting wood within reach.

directions: Mridula was bred at an Indian agricultural research station as an improvement on the older Ganesh cultivar and quickly became one of Maharashtra's major commercial pomegranates alongside Bhagwa and Ganesh. Fruit carries a deep red skin and deep red, soft-seeded arils with a sweeter, less tart flavor profile than Ganesh, and trees are notably more vigorous and productive than their parent. As with other Indian selections, Mridula rewards a hot, dry ripening season, so in humid Gulf Coast gardens prioritize full sun, sharp drainage, and generous spacing to reduce fungal pressure on ripening fruit. Expect several years of establishment growth before a substantial first harvest.
sources: Mahatma Phule Krishi Vidyapeeth (MPKV), Rahuri — Pomegranate Cultivar Records

planting.note: Plant rooted cuttings or container trees in spring; because the fruit grows unusually large and heavy, stake young leaders and thin excess fruit set to prevent limb breakage in later years.

directions: Kandahar is a historically significant Afghan pomegranate landrace named for the province where it has long been grown, and it is recognized by the international Slow Food Ark of Taste catalog for its exceptionally large fruit, which can weigh well over a pound apiece. Skin is deep red and the soft-seeded arils are notably sweet with balancing acidity, a flavor profile that made Afghan pomegranates historically prized as trade goods across Central and South Asia. It is a distinct regional selection from the unrelated 'Afghanistan' cultivar already grown elsewhere, having its own separate lineage tied specifically to Kandahar province orchards. Give it full sun and excellent drainage, and expect a long-lived, productive tree once past its multi-year establishment period.
sources: Slow Food Foundation for Biodiversity — Ark of Taste: Kandahar Pomegranate

planting.note: Plant rooted cuttings or container trees in spring; the notably early ripening window lets Gulf Coast growers harvest well ahead of typical fall-season pomegranate rains that can split or mold slower-ripening cultivars.

directions: Bred in Russia and named for its unusually early ripening, Sverkhranniy ('super early') produces medium-large red-and-pink fruit with sweet, soft-seeded arils by early August, well ahead of most other named pomegranate cultivars. Its Central Asian breeding background gives it above-average root cold-hardiness compared to warm-climate selections, though top growth still needs winter protection or dieback management outside its adapted zones. For Gulf Coast gardeners, the chief appeal is dodging the humid, rain-prone late-season window that causes fruit splitting and fungal spotting on later-ripening cultivars. Prune to an open, multi-trunk shrub form and thin fruit clusters to encourage larger individual fruit size.
sources: One Green World — Sverkhranniy Pomegranate

planting.note: Plant rooted cuttings or container trees in spring in full sun; this cultivar's relative tolerance of humid, subtropical conditions makes it a lower-maintenance alternative to drier-climate cultivars for Gulf South plantings.

directions: Spanish Ruby is an older American heirloom pomegranate long recommended by Gulf South and Florida extension programs as a dependable choice for humid subtropical growing conditions where premier California commercial cultivars are more prone to fruit splitting and rot. Fruit is medium-sized with ruby-red skin and juice, offering a balanced sweet-tart flavor suited to fresh eating and juicing alike. Its practical value lies less in exceptional size or sweetness than in consistent performance and better disease tolerance under rainy, high-humidity conditions than many showier named cultivars. Site it in full sun with good air movement and well-drained soil for the healthiest fruit set.
sources: Texas A&M AgriLife Extension — Pomegranates for Texas
University of Florida IFAS Extension — The Pomegranate

planting.note: Plant rooted cuttings or container plants in spring; the compact habit and quick bearing age make Haku-Botan one of the better pomegranate cultivars for large containers or small dooryard beds.

directions: A Japanese heirloom cultivar, Haku-Botan is grown for its showy double white flowers with a faint yellow blush as much as for its fruit, and it stays notably more compact than standard orchard pomegranates. Unlike the strictly ornamental dwarf 'Nana' type, Haku-Botan reliably produces medium fruit with pale greenish-yellow skin and white to pale pink arils carrying a mild, low-acid flavor. It bears at a young age, often within one to two years, and its small stature suits patio containers or tight garden beds where a full-sized pomegranate would outgrow the space. Give it full sun and well-drained soil, and expect both a longer ornamental bloom season and a lighter, milder-tasting harvest than heavier-bearing commercial cultivars.
sources: One Green World — Haku-Botan White Pomegranate
